rows: Long call
Buy 1 call
Unlimited (the stock can keep rising)
The premium paid
The price will rise, and rise enough to cover the premium before expiry.
Needs a move, not just the right direction. A stock that drifts up slowly can still lose money because time decay eats the premium.
Long put
Buy 1 put
Large but bounded (the stock cannot fall below zero)
The premium paid
The price will fall, and fall enough to cover the premium before expiry.
Falling volatility hurts even when the direction is right - the put loses value if the market calms down.
Covered call
Own the stock, sell 1 call
Premium plus the gain up to the strike
The stock can fall to zero, less the premium received
Mildly bullish or flat - happy to sell the upside for income.
Caps the upside. If the stock doubles, you keep only up to the strike. The premium is small compared with the downside you still carry.
Protective put
Own the stock, buy 1 put
Unlimited (the stock can keep rising)
The fall to the strike, plus the premium
Bullish but wanting a floor under the position.
Insurance costs money every time. Held for long, the premiums can add up to more than the protection ever pays.
Bull call spread
Buy a lower-strike call, sell a higher-strike call
The gap between strikes, less the net premium
The net premium paid
Moderately bullish - up, but not beyond the upper strike.
Selling the second leg cuts the cost and caps the gain. Cheaper than a long call and also worth less if the move is large.
Bear put spread
Buy a higher-strike put, sell a lower-strike put
The gap between strikes, less the net premium
The net premium paid
Moderately bearish - down, but not below the lower strike.
The mirror of the bull call spread. A crash pays no more than a modest fall.
Long straddle
Buy 1 call and 1 put at the same strike
Unlimited in theory, in either direction
Both premiums
A big move is coming, but not which way.
You pay for two options and need a large move just to break even. If the market stays quiet, both legs decay at once.
Long strangle
Buy an out-of-the-money call and an out-of-the-money put
Unlimited in theory, in either direction
Both premiums
A big move is coming, and cheaply expressed.
Cheaper than a straddle and needs an even larger move to pay. This is the structure behind most very cheap options.
Iron condor
Sell a call spread and sell a put spread, both out of the money
The net premium received
The wider spread, less the premium
The price will stay inside a range.
Wins often and small, loses rarely and large. The shape that makes people believe they have found an edge, right up until one bad week.
Short straddle
Sell 1 call and 1 put at the same strike
Both premiums
Unlimited on the call side
The price will stay near the strike.
The exact opposite of a long straddle, and the risk profile is not symmetrical - the loss has no ceiling. Most exchanges require large margin for this reason.
note: Each row is a payoff shape, not a recommendation. Which structure suits anyone depends on capital, risk tolerance and what they expect - none of which this page can know.

cautions.sebi: SEBI's own studies have found most individual F&O traders lose money over time. Every structure above is arithmetic; none of it changes those odds.
cautions.premium_is_not_cost: Premium x lot size is what leaves your account, plus brokerage, STT, exchange charges and GST.
cautions.time_decay: Every bought option loses value as expiry approaches, whether or not the price moves. That is why being right on direction is not enough.
cautions.not_advice: This is educational reference only. It is not investment advice, not a recommendation, and not a signal.
